opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is that, today, the cost of a model is no longer dominated by training. It's dominated by serving. Once a model is deployed, it might be called billions of times, and every architectural decision you make at design time becomes a recurring cost at inference time. So if the people designing the model don't understand how it will actually run on hardware, they can easily make choices that look elegant on paper but are very expensive in practice.

Let me give a concrete example. Take attention. In the standard multi-head attention, the KV cache grows with sequence length, number of layers, and number of heads. During decoding, you're mostly memory-bandwidth bound: for every token you generate, you have to read the whole KV cache from GPU memory. So the size of the KV cache directly determines how many requests you can batch together and how fast each token comes out. That's why we've seen ideas like multi-query attention, grouped-query attention, and more recently things like multi-head latent attention, where the KV cache is compressed into a low-rank latent. These are architecture changes, but the motivation is purely an inference-system motivation. They only make sense if you think about memory bandwidth and batching.

Mixture-of-experts is another good example. From a modeling point of view, MoE lets you scale parameters without scaling compute per token. But in serving, it introduces a whole new set of problems: expert parallelism, all-to-all communication, load imbalance between experts, how you place experts across GPUs or across nodes. If you choose the number of experts, the top-k, or the expert size without thinking about the cluster topology and the interconnect bandwidth, you might end up with a model that's theoretically efficient but in practice bottlenecked on communication. The teams that do this well, they really co-design: they pick expert counts and granularity that match the hardware, and they design routing with load balancing in mind.

And it goes the other way, too. Inference infrastructure shouldn't just passively accept whatever architecture comes along. From working on vLLM, one thing I've seen is that every new model brings new requirements: sliding-window attention, hybrid models mixing attention with linear attention or state-space layers, different KV cache layouts, multimodal encoders. If the inference engine is designed too rigidly around one architecture, it can't keep up. So we've had to make the system more modular and general, for example with abstractions for the KV cache manager that can handle different kinds of layers, and things like torch.compile integration so we can optimize new architectures without hand-writing everything. But even with a flexible system, the best outcomes come when model developers talk to the infrastructure people early, before the architecture is frozen.

There's also a hardware dimension. Different accelerators have different ratios of compute to memory bandwidth, different interconnects, different support for low-precision formats like FP8 or FP4. An architecture that's optimal on one generation of GPUs may not be optimal on the next. So co-design is really a three-way thing: model, system, and hardware.

So my view is: in the era where inference is the main cost and the main user experience, whether that's latency for chat, or throughput for agents and reasoning models that generate very long outputs, you simply can't treat model architecture and inference infrastructure as separate problems. The architecture defines what's possible to optimize, and the infrastructure defines what's actually affordable to deploy. Designing them together is how you get models that are not just smart, but also cheap and fast enough for people to actually use.

fable-5.1.text:
Because in practice, the two have never really been separate. When I work on vLLM, what I see every day is that the cost of serving a model is decided long before anyone writes an inference engine. It's decided when someone picks the attention variant, the KV cache layout, the number of experts, the vocabulary size. Those choices determine how much memory bandwidth you need per token, how well you can batch requests, whether you can overlap communication with compute. If the architecture team makes those decisions in isolation, we on the infrastructure side end up spending months building workarounds for problems that could have been avoided with a small change upfront.

A simple example is the KV cache. The whole idea of paged attention came from noticing that memory for the cache was being wasted. But if you think about it, that waste is an architectural property as much as a systems one. Multi-query attention, grouped-query attention, multi-head latent attention in DeepSeek, these are all architecture decisions that exist largely because people were thinking about inference cost. The teams that made those changes had infrastructure people in the room, or they were the infrastructure people themselves.

The other direction matters too. Infrastructure shapes what architectures are even viable. Mixture of experts only makes sense if you can route tokens efficiently across devices. Speculative decoding only helps if the serving system can verify drafts cheaply. If the infrastructure can't support an idea at scale, that idea stays in a paper. So the co-design isn't a nice-to-have. It's the difference between a model that's impressive in a benchmark table and a model that people can actually afford to run.

I'd put it this way: the model is the interface between what the research team wants and what the hardware can give. Designing one side without the other is like designing a car engine without knowing whether it's going in a truck or a motorcycle. You can do it, but you won't be happy with the result.

astra-6.text:
Because the architecture determines what the inference system has to do, and the inference system determines whether that architecture is actually efficient in practice. You can reduce the number of operations on paper, but if the resulting model moves more data or needs more communication between devices, it might run slower.

Attention is a good example. The way you design attention affects how much state you cache during generation. That affects memory usage, how many requests you can serve together, and ultimately latency and throughput. So an architectural choice becomes a serving decision as well.

And the feedback goes in both directions. If you understand where the inference system spends its time, you can design the model to avoid those bottlenecks. The goal is to get the best model quality within a real latency, memory, and cost budget. To do that, you need to think about the model and the system together.

sol-6.1.text:
I think architecture defines the work you need to do, but inference infrastructure determines how efficiently you can actually do it. So if you design them separately, you can end up optimizing the wrong thing.

For example, an architectural change might reduce the number of computations, but introduce more memory movement or communication between GPUs. On paper it looks cheaper; in practice it may be slower. And the reverse is also true: an architecture that looks more expensive can run efficiently if the infrastructure has good support for its operations.

The workload matters, too. Processing a long prompt and generating tokens one at a time have different bottlenecks. Batching, caching, and parallelism all affect which architectural choices make sense.

So I see it as a feedback loop. You design the model, measure it in a realistic serving environment, and use those results to improve both the architecture and the infrastructure. The goal is model quality at a useful latency and cost, rather than optimizing either side in isolation.
